config.title: Utility Types

intro.title: Utility Types
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular component that uses TypeScript utility types to manage and transform user data. You will learn how utility types like Partial, Readonly, and Pick help you create flexible and type-safe code by modifying existing types. The main technologies involved are Angular components and TypeScript's built-in utility types. By the end, you'll understand how to apply these types to make your Angular applications more robust and maintainable.
intro.usecase: Utility Types are essential for managing complex data in real-world Angular applications, such as admin dashboards where user data must be selectively displayed or updated. For instance, when building a user profile form, developers can use `Partial<T>` to allow incremental updates without requiring all fields, or `Pick<T>` to extract specific properties for a summary panel. In interactive UI components like data tables with filters, `Omit<T>` helps create safe payloads by excluding internal IDs before sending data to an API. Mastering these types ensures type safety, reduces runtime errors, and streamlines development in scenarios like dynamic forms, API integrations, and state management.

objectives: Apply the `Partial<T>` utility type to create flexible form interfaces.
Construct read-only data structures using the `Readonly<T>` utility type.
Implement the `Pick<T, K>` utility type to extract specific properties from an interface.
Manipulate object types by omitting properties with the `Omit<T, K>` utility type.
Integrate the `Record<K, T>` utility type to define typed dictionaries or maps.
Update existing types by making properties optional or required with `Partial<T>` and `Required<T>`.
Configure component inputs using utility types to enforce type safety in Angular templates.

steps.title: Import Angular core and create component
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and create a basic component class named UtilityTypesDemo with a @Component decorator that has an empty template and selector 'app-utility-types-demo'.
steps.hint: Start by importing Component, then use @Component decorator on a class. The template can be empty for now.
steps.seedCode: // Import Component from '@angular/core' and create the component class
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a basic Angular component structure ready to build upon.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and a class named UtilityTypesDemo with @Component decorator (selector: 'app-utility-types-demo', template: '') is created.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you imported Component and created the class with the @Component decorator.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statement and component class syntax. You need to import Component and apply the decorator.

steps.title: Define interface for user data
steps.instruction: Inside your component class, create a TypeScript interface named User with id (number), name (string), email (string), and optional age (number) properties.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions. For optional properties, add a '?' after the property name.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface is defined with the required properties, providing type safety for user data in your component.
successCriteria: The User interface exists with id: number, name: string, email: string, and optional age?: number properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your User interface includes all required properties: id (number), name (string), email (string), and optional age (number).
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface is not properly defined. Check that you used the 'interface' keyword and included all required properties with correct TypeScript types.

steps.title: Initialize user data with Partial utility
steps.instruction: Inside the UtilityTypesComponent class, create a property called 'userData' with the type 'Partial<User>' and initialize it as an empty object.
steps.hint: Use the Partial utility type to make all properties from the User interface optional, then assign an empty object {} to it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a userData property typed as Partial<User> that can hold partial user data for updates.
successCriteria: The UtilityTypesComponent class contains a 'userData' property with type 'Partial<User>' initialized to an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared 'userData' with the correct type 'Partial<User>' and initialized it as an empty object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The userData property is missing or incorrectly typed. It should be declared as 'userData: Partial<User> = {}' inside the component class.

steps.title: Create readonly user with Readonly utility
steps.instruction: In the UtilityTypesComponent class, add a property named readonlyUser with the type Readonly<User> and assign it a user object with name 'Jane Doe' and age 30.
steps.hint: Use the Readonly<User> type annotation for the readonlyUser property. This will make all properties of the user object immutable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The readonlyUser property will be created with the Readonly<User> type, demonstrating how to make an object immutable in TypeScript.
successCriteria: The readonlyUser property is defined with type Readonly<User> and initialized with a valid user object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the readonlyUser property, but check that it uses the Readonly<User> type and is initialized with a valid user object containing name and age.
steps.feedbackWrong: The readonlyUser property is missing or incorrectly defined. Make sure to use Readonly<User> as the type and provide a valid user object with name and age properties.

steps.title: Extract subset with Pick utility
steps.instruction: Inside the UtilityTypesComponent class, add a new property called 'userContact' with the type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and initialize it with an object containing name and email values.
steps.hint: Use the Pick utility type to create a type that includes only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a userContact property with a type that includes only the name and email properties from the User interface.
successCriteria: The userContact property is defined with type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and initialized with an object containing name and email values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct syntax for Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and initializing the object with both name and email properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The userContact property should be defined with type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and initialized with an object containing name and email values.

steps.title: Create required user with Required utility
steps.instruction: Add a property named 'completeUser' to your component class. Use the Required<User> utility type to make all properties from the User interface required, and initialize it with a complete user object.
steps.hint: The Required utility type removes optional modifiers from all properties. You'll need to provide values for all properties defined in your User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a completeUser property that uses the Required<User> type to enforce all properties as required.
successCriteria: A completeUser property is added to the component class with the Required<User> type and initialized with a complete user object containing all required properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the Required<User> type and providing values for all properties from your User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a completeUser property using Required<User> type with all properties from your User interface.

steps.title: Add template structure for displaying data
steps.instruction: Replace the existing template with a structured template that includes sections to display each utility type example. Create a main container with headings and paragraphs for each property.
steps.hint: Replace the entire template string with a structured template containing divs, h2/h3 headings, and p tags to display each property value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template will have a structured layout with sections for each utility type example, ready to display data when properties are added.
successCriteria: Template contains structured sections with headings and paragraphs for displaying utility type examples
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the template structure, but make sure to include all the sections needed for the utility type examples. Check that you have headings and paragraphs for each property we'll display.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template structure doesn't match the expected format. You need to replace the existing template with a structured template containing sections for each utility type example.

steps.title: Display utility type examples in template
steps.instruction: Update the template to display the properties of each utility type object using interpolation.
steps.hint: Use double curly braces {{ }} to bind each property value to the template. Display each object's properties in separate paragraphs or divs.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will show the actual property values from each utility type object instead of just the placeholder text.
successCriteria: Template contains interpolation expressions showing properties from userData, readonlyUser, userContact, userWithoutId, and completeUser objects.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some interpolation, but make sure to display properties from all five utility type objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't yet display the utility type objects. Use interpolation with double curly braces {{ }} to show property values.

steps.title: Add explanatory comments and finalize
steps.instruction: Add explanatory comments above each property in the component class to briefly explain what each utility type does.
steps.hint: Add a single-line comment (//) or multi-line comment (/* */) above each property to describe the utility type's purpose.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have comments explaining each utility type example, making the code self-documenting.
successCriteria: Comments are added above each property explaining the utility type's purpose (Partial, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Required).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some comments, but make sure to add explanatory comments for all utility type properties (Partial, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Required).
steps.feedbackWrong: The comments are missing or don't explain the utility types. Add comments above each property to describe what each utility type does.
